analysis.one_liner: Suspends and forgives rent and mortgage payments for primary homes during COVID, repaying landlords and lenders in full.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote, floor vote, or any action beyond its referral in the House, and died when the 117th Congress ended; all 27 of its cosponsors were Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have suspended all rent and mortgage payments on primary residences during the COVID-19 emergency, erased rent and mortgage debt that piled up from March 2020 through April 2022, and barred late fees, evictions, foreclosures, and credit-score damage for nonpayment. To soften the blow, it would have created federal funds to reimburse landlords and mortgage lenders dollar-for-dollar for everything they didn't collect, in exchange for five-year rent freezes, just-cause eviction rules, and detailed ownership disclosures. It also would have given nonprofits, public housing agencies, community land trusts, and local governments the first chance to buy large apartment buildings that went up for sale, to keep them out of corporate investors' hands. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Every household renting or paying a mortgage on a primary residence — roughly all of them nationwide — would have had payments suspended and back debt from the pandemic erased, with no late fees, no eviction or foreclosure for nonpayment, and no hit to their credit. Tenant households that had already paid rent during the covered period would have been reimbursed. Nonprofit and community buyers of large apartment buildings would have gained a first right of purchase.

how_it_helps.text: Rent and mortgage payments on primary residences were suspended for the COVID-19 suspension period, and no tenant could be fined, evicted, or reported to credit agencies for nonpayment [S2] [S3].
All residential rent and mortgage arrears that accrued from March 13, 2020 through April 1, 2022 were to be forgiven, with state and local laws that conflict preempted [S2] [S3].

Tenants who took adverse action against tenants for exercising these rights would face civil penalties starting at $5,000 and rising to $50,000 or forfeiture of the property, with attorney's fees awarded to winning plaintiffs [S3].
HUD would reimburse landlords and lenders for suspended or forgiven payments, and repay tenants and homeowners who had already paid during the covered period [S2] [S3].

A new Affordable Housing Acquisition Fund would finance acquisitions of multifamily buildings by nonprofits, public housing agencies, cooperatives, community land trusts, and state and local governments, giving them a first right of purchase for five years to prevent a repeat of the corporate buyups that followed the 2008 crisis [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through HUD funds authorized at 'such sums as may be necessary' to repay landlords and lenders for roughly two years of suspended rent and mortgage payments nationwide — an open-ended cost in the hundreds of billions of dollars. Landlords and lenders who accepted reimbursement would bear conditions: a five-year rent freeze, just-cause eviction, and tracing ownership down to natural persons.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, via open-ended HUD funds

drawbacks.text: The reimbursement funds are authorized at 'such sums as may be necessary' with no dollar cap, so the full cost of suspending rent and mortgage payments for every primary residence in America for roughly two years would fall on taxpayers [S3].

Relief would be universal rather than targeted: a homeowner with no income loss would get the same debt forgiveness as a household facing eviction, making the program far more expensive than need-based aid [S3].

Landlords and lenders are made financially whole, so the bill's benefits to households come entirely from federal spending rather than from the property and lending industries absorbing any loss; accepting industries would take on significant new conditions, including a five-year rent freeze, just-cause evictions, and disclosure of every layer of ownership down to individual people [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to households — a clean slate on pandemic-era housing debt with no evictions, foreclosures, or credit damage — would have been very large. But the design is expensive and blunt: the government reimburses landlords and lenders in full, the relief is universal rather than targeted to people who actually lost income, and the open-ended appropriation makes the fiscal cost hard to bound. An honest supporter would concede that a narrower, means-tested version could deliver most of the protection at a fraction of the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the Rent and Mortgage Cancellation Act of 2021 on March 11, 2021 with 27 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction [S2] [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history — no committee markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords, mortgage lenders, and servicers are better off: they kept collecting rent and mortgage payments through the pandemic without a five-year rent freeze, just-cause eviction rules, or disclosure of their full ownership structures. Taxpayers also avoided what would have been an open-ended federal outlay.

for.name: 27 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 27 were Democrats.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 11, 2021 and took no further action; the bill was never marked up or voted on.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; all 27 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican supported the bill [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have paid landlords dollar-for-dollar for every suspended or forgiven rent payment, so they would not have lost money — but only by accepting a five-year rent freeze, just-cause eviction, source-of-income protections, and disclosure of ownership down to natural persons, which is why the industry-oriented alternative was the status quo. Because the bill died, landlords kept full control with no new conditions.

Lenders would have been fully reimbursed for suspended and forgiven mortgage payments, with no added interest, fees, or foreclosures allowed — but in exchange they would have faced detailed fair-lending reporting and ownership disclosure requirements. The bill's death left lending practices untouched.

The bill would have given nonprofits, land trusts, and public agencies a first right of purchase on apartment buildings for five years, explicitly to prevent a repeat of the 2008-style corporate buyup of rental housing. The bill's death removed that barrier.
Nonpayment and forgiveness could not have been reported or counted against anyone's credit score, cutting off a stream of housing payment data.
